title: Generic logic block based on bias-gated 2D MoS_2 transistors

paper_content.abstract: Integrating two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors and CMOS technology is a promising pathway for next-generation integrated circuits. However, the implementation of this strategy is hindered by the limited polarity modulation of 2D semiconductors and the inherent characteristics of CMOS architectures. Here, we report a generic logic block (GLB) that uses bias-gated molybdenum disulfide transistors (BG-FET). The BG-FETs exhibit threshold-adaptive field-effect characteristics through simple bias manipulation, enabling good rail-to-rail operation in the inverter circuits. The GLB composed of four BG-FETs can perform reconfigurable logic operations in a single circuit, including basic gate circuits, half-adder, multiplexer, encoder and static-random-access-memory. In contrast, conventional CMOS circuits require at least 100 transistors to perform the same set of operations. We further integrate flip-flop circuits and arithmetic logic units by cascading as-fabricated GLBs, featuring a transistor count saving of over 60% compared to CMOS design. Collectively, BG-FET-based GLB emerges as a post-CMOS integration technology with compelling potential.
paper_content.introduction:
Two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors still maintain excellent electrical characteristics even at sub-nanometer scales and offer the potential for further extending the logic device scaling1-6. But its potential is severely hampered by the lack of proper logic architecture. The current silicon-based CMOS (complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor) architecture realized by high-energy doping technology is not suitable for atomically thin 2D semiconductors. So far, various doping methods have been developed to tune the polarity of 2D transistors7-9. But effective techniques towards practical circuit-level manufacture still lack because there is little physical space for impurity dopants in such atomically thin lattice10. Therefore, most large-scale logic circuits based on 2D semiconductors developed to date primarily follow the non-complementary NMOS architecture11-14, which inherently exhibit higher power consumption than CMOS technology. More importantly, an inherent problem is that logic functions implemented in CMOS or NMOS architecture require a large number of transistors, which hinders the processes of chip area scaling-down and function integration. Consequently, a necessity has been awakened to develop integrated device architectures based on the intrinsic advantages of 2D materials.

The emerging reconfigurable technology15, in which a transistor can be dynamically programmed to function as either an n- or p-FET during run-time by applying an external control voltage, presents a promising approach beyond CMOS. Reconfigurable circuits can achieve higher logic function density compared to CMOS architecture, thereby improving transistor utilization and reducing circuit redundancy. However, the reconfigurable field-effect transistor (RFET) relies on the modulation of device polarity, transitioning from ambipolar type to either n- or p- type, which necessitates additional hardware resources to implement16-19. This will result in additional power consumption and problems with circuit complexity. Moreover, the implementation of Boolean functions in the RFET-based circuits with full-swing output still follows a CMOS-like configuration20, utilizing p-FETs and n-FETs for pull-up and pull-down networks, respectively. This approach does not contribute to reducing the overall transistor count. Alternatively, reconfigurable circuit elements based on 2D homo- or heterostructure device21-23 and 2D single-transistor-based logic elements using a vertical- or split-dual-gate design24-27 are widely recognized as effective strategies to simplify circuits. However, these reconfigurable circuits are limited to small set of few fundamental logic operations and are further constrained by the intrinsic polarity or thickness of 2D semiconductors.

In this article, we report a bias-gated FET (BG-FET, Fig. 1a) designed to integrate generic logic blocks (GLBs). The asymmetric bias-gated device architecture enables BG-FETs to possess threshold-adaptive field-effect characteristics through different bias modes (source-gated or drain-gated, Fig. 1b). Leveraging these unique structural and electrical features, firstly, a cascaded logic inverter consisting of two BG-FETs with identical process parameters is fabricated to achieve good rail-to-rail operation. Subsequently, within a circuit composed of four BG-FETs, we design and fabricate a GLB with full-equivalent input/output (I/O) ports for performing dynamic reconfigurable logic computing by programming different combinations of input signals (Fig. 1c), including basic gate circuits, half-adder, multiplexer (MUX), encoder and static random-access memory (SRAM). As a benchmark comparison, implementing these functions in CMOS design typically requires more than 100 transistors (Fig. 1d). The as-fabricated GLBs are further used to integrate multiple arithmetic logic units and sequential circuit units with a transistor count reduction of over 60% compared to CMOS design, such as 2-bit multipliers and edge-triggered flip-flops.
paper_content.results:
Characterization of the unipolar MoS BG-FET
2
A schematic of the BG-FET device concept is shown in Fig. 2a. The basic structure consists of a unipolar CVD-grown monolayer MoS channel sandwiched between hafnium oxide and antimony oxide (HfO /MoS /Sb O /HfO ), as well as a fully back-gated bottom electrode and a locally unilateral bias-gated top electrode. To confirm the signature device structure of our BG-FET, a representative sample and a traditional MOSFET for reference (Ref. FET) are simultaneously fabricated based on a same MoS film (Fig. 2b). The fabrication processes (see in Methods) of two devices are completely identical, except that an asymmetrically extended bias-gated electrode is added to the BG-FET. Notably, we choose a van der Waals crystal Sb O as a buffer layer to form a high-quality oxide-to-semiconductor interface28-30, enabling the integration of high-κ dielectrics via atomic layer deposition. Moreover, a van der Waals gate dielectric interface can better maintain the intrinsic properties of the underlying 2D materials, which also helpful for improving the uniformity and stability of 2D electronics.

The asymmetrical nature of this as-fabricated BG-FET is defined as two different bias schemes: extended bias-gated electrode as source (named source-gated, S-Gated) and as drain (named drain-gated, D-Gated). In principle, the energy band diagrams under two operating modes are shown in Fig. 2c. In S-Gated mode, the channel electrons around the source contact are depleted due to the bias-gated electrostatic (negative potential relative to the drain), resulting in the extension of the electron injection barrier compared to the Ref. FET. The widened barrier can block the injection of electrons from the source, thus requiring a larger V . In D-Gated mode, the accumulated electrons can improve the channel conductivity around the drain contact due to the bias-gated electrostatic (positive potential relative to the source), but not affecting the electron injection barrier at the source.

In detailed comparison, the electrical properties of two devices are investigated under the same testing conditions. As shown in Fig. 2d, the saturation voltage (V ) of BG-FET is smaller under the same gate voltage (V ) compared with the Ref. FET. By definition, the V corresponds to the drain-source voltage (V ) at which the drain-source current (I ) reaches saturation, equivalent to the V required for transistor pinch-off. Figure 2e illustrates the pinch-off mechanism of BG-FET and Ref. FET. As V increases, the depletion region of Ref. FET occurs at drain until the channel is pinched off and V is defined. In S-Gated mode, however, the depletion of BG-FET occurs both in drain and source due to the extended bias-gated electrode31,32. The source-side depletion region progressively expands towards the drain with the increasing V due to the bias-gated electrostatic (maintained at a negative potential relative to the drain), enabling the BG-FET to be pinched off prematurely and a smaller V is defined. Figure 2f exhibits the transfer characteristics of two devices both with a high on-off ratio of >109 and a low off-state current of less than 0.1 pA. Noticeably, the V (reference voltage, defined as the V required when the I is equal to 1 nA) in S-Gated mode is offset by around 0.7 V in the forward (right) direction compared to Ref. FET. A larger V for BG-FET is required to achieve the same current due to the bias-gated device structure. The maximum difference of I under the same V exceeds three orders of magnitude in the sub-threshold region. As the V increases, this difference gradually decreases and tends to be consistent, because the electron density in the channel is gradually dominated by V . The V -dependent V , R and more experimental data of two devices are demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. 1. These obvious differences between two devices indicate the effectiveness of the bias-gated structure design.

More valuable is that the asymmetric bias-gated device architecture enables BG-FETs to possess threshold-adaptive field-effect characteristics, which is crucial for subsequent GLB circuit design. To verify the inherent robustness of this characteristic and assess its scalability for large-scale integration, we fabricate an array of 256 BG-FETs distributed across 16 dies, with each die integrating 16 individual devices (Supplementary Fig. 2). All devices were fabricated on a continuous single-crystal MoS₂ thin film33 under identical process parameters. Subsequently, four BG-FETs were randomly selected from four units in each die for electrical characterization, yielding a total of 64 devices spread out to study uniformity over a large area. The transfer characteristics of BG-FETs under D-Gated and S-Gated modes are tested, as shown in Fig. 2g. The transistors exhibit a desired uniformity and threshold-adaptive field-effect characteristics. Besides, the statistical histogram of V difference in two modes is concentrated between 0.54-0.6 V (see the inset of Fig. 2g), indicating a low device-to-device variability.

To further explore the stability of BG-FETs, we electrically characterized the as-fabricated devices placed in the vacuum atmosphere for 1 week, 4 weeks, and 7 weeks. As shown in Fig. 2h, the BG-FET maintain excellent threshold-adaptive field-effect characteristics after seven weeks, and the ΔV of approximately 0.57 V between the two operating modes shows negligible variation throughout this period. And the BG-FET exhibit impressive threshold-adaptive field-effect characteristics even at high temperature of 400 K, as shown in Fig. 2i. Note that the threshold voltage of the BG-FET exhibits a negative shift with increasing temperature. This phenomenon can be attributed to the enhanced thermal activation of free carriers at elevated temperatures34,35. Furthermore, a larger shift amplitude is observed in S-Gated mode, leading to a progressive decrease in ΔV . This may be due to the release of more free carriers bound by the widened barrier induced by bias-gated electrostatic at high temperatures. The desired uniformity and stability of BG-FETs can be attributed to the bias-gated structure design with a built-in packaging function for maintaining the integrity of the channel materials, except for the high stability of the grown MoS .

Logic inverter based on unipolar MoS BG-FET
2
The inverter (NOT gate) that performs the Boolean function Y = A̅ is a basic logic element in digital circuits, in which A̅ is defined as an opposite voltage level to input A. Figure 3a shows the schematic of an adaptive-switching logic inverter composed of two as-fabricated unipolar MoS BG-FETs in series. In reported MoS -based inverter circuits11,12,36,37, specific designs are required for the driver and load devices to achieve rail-to-rail operation, such as different width/length (W/L) ratios, metal gates or channel materials between two transistors. In our demonstration, the as-fabricated SG-FET as driver (BG-FET in S-Gated mode) and DG-FET as load (BG-FET in D-Gated mode) can be dynamically switched through simple voltage manipulation.

To further clarify the role of a bias-gated device structure in digital circuits, two inverters made of BG-FETs and Ref. FETs are fabricated, respectively (Fig. 3b). The four devices used to fabricate two inverters have the same size and are based on a same single-layer MoS . Figure 3c shows the typical voltage transfer curves (VTCs) of two inverters with different switching threshold voltage (V ) at V = 2 V. The V of the BG-FET-based inverter (BG-inverter) shifts from approximately -0.15 V to 0.59 V compared with Ref. FET-based inverter (Ref.-inverter), which indicates that BG-inverter can realize good rail-to-rail operation due to the threshold-adaptive field-effect characteristics of BG-FET. Noticeably, an inverter that loses the cascaded function due to input and output not in the same range is strictly referred to as an invalid circuit. As mentioned above, the reported inverters require a specific design to achieve rail-to-rail operation, however, which cannot change the function of the constituent components (load or driver) once built.

More detailed static characteristics of the BG-inverter and Ref. inverter under different V are shown in Supplementary Fig. 3. Two inverters show similar performance for the parameters of gain and I across all V values. Where a peak gain of 157 for BG-inverter and of 159 for Ref. inverter, a peak I of less than 2 nA for BG-inverter and of less than 5 nA for Ref. inverter are achieved at V = 5 V. And the key parameters of BG-inverter, such as peak gain, V , noise margin (N /V ) and peak static power are intuitively shown in Fig. 3d-e. A total noise margin (NM + NM )/V over 85% and a low static power (P ) of less than 10 nW across all V values are calculated. And The V shift of 0.06 V for BG-inverter under different V is observed, which may be attributed to the ΔV variation of BG-FET under different V . In theory, the competition relationship between bias-gated and back-gated modulation can be controlled by optimizing the L /L ratios, in which L and L are defined as the length of the bias-gated electrode and the channel in Fig. 2a, respectively. As this ratio increases, the control region of the bias-gated electrode expands relatively. The controllable modulation of this competition relationship allows for the on-demand design of application-oriented devices.

Additionally, the BG-inverter can maintain a full-swing output response at a 2 V full-scale square input signal of 100 Hz, even after 1,000 switching cycles (Figure 3f). The dynamic switching speed mainly determined by the RC delay (𝜏) is also a very significant evaluation indicator in logic circuits. To further characterize this performance, the dynamic switching behavior of the BG-inverter by using an AC input signal is studied at higher frequencies (Supplementary Fig. 4). As demonstrated by the dynamic analysis, the inverter can immediately invert the input signal, and the output signal can maintain a high-quality waveform response that is opposite to the input signal at a relatively low frequency (<500 Hz). However, the output waveform gradually deformed with the frequency of the input signal increases, and full-swing output cannot be achieved at a higher frequency (>5 kHz) mainly due to a RC delay in dynamic switching. A rising time delay (𝜏 ) of 285 µs and falling time delay (𝜏 ) of 35 µs are extracted at 1 kHz, where the delay 𝜏 is defined as the time intervals between 10% and 90% of V , as shown in Fig. 3g. These performance metrics of the BG-inverters demonstrate competitive results at the current device scale compared with state-of-the-art 2D materials-based CMOS inverters (Supplementary Table 1). There remains significant potential for further optimization through continued device engineering and process refinement.

Generic logic block based on unipolar MoS BG -FET
2N
Figure 4a schematically depicts the circuit design diagram of a generic logic block (GLB) with a specific cascade mode based on four BG-FETs. This GLB can perform logic functions with six input terminals (V , V , V , V , V and V̅̅̅̅̅̅) and two output terminals (V and V ). The bias-gated source-drain is set as the pass-input terminal (V ), the non-bias-gated source-drain is set as the output terminal (V ), and the gate is set as the control-input terminal (V ). Note that the manufacturing process parameters of four BG-FETs used to fabricate the GLB are almost identical (as shown in Fig. 4b), and they can all dynamically switch between D-Gated mode and S-Gated mode through simple voltage manipulation (Fig. 4c). These features mean that four V ports of the as-fabricated GLB are fully equivalent, which is crucial for GLB to perform arbitrary logic operations in a same circuit. For example, the Boolean function for basic gate circuits (AND/NAND, OR/NOR, and XOR/XNOR), arithmetic unit (half-adder and 2:1 MUX) and memory cell (SRAM) can be achieved in a single GLB circuit by programming the combinations of input signals (as shown in Fig. 4d). The measured output waveforms driven by programming schemes and input combinations are shown in Fig. 4e, achieving a dynamic reconfigurable computing paradigm. Here, the high voltage level (2 V) is defined as logic ‘1’ and the low voltage level (0 V) is defined as logic ‘0’. The implementation of more details is shown in Supplementary Fig. 5-7.

In addition, the GLB can be reconstructed to a 4-2 encoder (a circuit that encodes 2n input signals using n-bit binary code) according the programming scheme shown in Fig. 4d. When V is set to A , V is set to A , V and V is set to A , V is set to A̅̅̅, V is set to Y , and V is set to Y , the GLB can perform the function of encoding 4-bit binary code (A , A , A , A ) with 2-bit binary code (Y , Y ). The measured result at a constraint condition (only one of the four signals A , A , A and A is set as logic ‘1’ at the same time) and a hidden condition (when A , A and A are all set as logic ‘0’, it means A is set as logic ‘1’) is shown in Fig. 4f. In this circuit, the 4-bit input signals: (0001), (0010), (0100), and (1000) are encoded as 2-bit binary codes: (00), (01), (10), and (11), respectively, which are consistent with the function truth table of the 4-2 encoder (Supplementary Fig. 8). Similarly, GLB can also be reconstructed as a 2-4 decoder (a circuit that decodes n-bit binary code into 2n-bit signals) that function exactly opposites to the encoder (Supplementary Fig. 9). Noteworthy, the GLB circuit can fully implement all logic functions with a full-swing output voltage due to the threshold-adaptive field-effect characteristics of BG-FET. The principle is analogous to the complementary structure in CMOS technology. More detailed explanation seen in Supplementary Fig. 10.

GLB-based digital circuits
To further verify the feasibility of GLB using BG-FET device architecture for digital circuit optimization, various arithmetic logic units (ALU) and sequential circuit units are integrated on the monolayer MoS film. Figure 5a shows the schematics and optical image of a 2-bit carry-save-adder (CSA) multiplier that consists of four GLBs and four BG-inverters with 24 BG-FETs in total. By analyzing the principle of multiplication (depicted in Supplementary Fig. 11a), it is found that the partial products can be achieved through logic AND gates (Y = AB). While the sum of partial products can be achieved through adder circuits. Based on this principle, two GLBs are reconstructed as four AND gates to implement four partial products, two GLBs are reconstructed as two half-adders for partial product summation and four embedded BG-inverters are used to provide necessary complementary signals. The measured output voltage signals (P , P , P , P ) are shown in Fig. 5b, indicating that GLB-based 2-bit CSA-multiplier can fully implement multiplication operations according to the truth table (shown in Supplementary Fig. 11b) for all the input combinations (A , A , B , B ). CSA multiplier circuits that can improve the speed of data processing and enable more complex data analysis with efficient computing play an important part in digital ICs. Furthermore, the circuit design, optical image and measured results for 1-bit digital comparator, controllable left/right shifter and 1-bit full-adder based on BG-FETs are also plotted as examples in Supplementary Fig. 12. The output voltage signals can correctly respond to all possible input combinations according to the truth table.

The sequential logic elements are critical components in memory and data manipulation circuits for digital ICs. Figure 5c shows the status table of D latch, D flip-flop (DFF) and T flip-flop (TFF), in which signal CLK as the global clock control input, signal D as the data input and signal Q as the output. The circuit design, optical image and measured waveforms of the D latch based on two BG-FETs and a SRAM reconstructed by GLB are plotted in Fig. 5d. In this sequential circuit, the output Qn+1 is seen to follow the input D when the input CLK is in logic ‘0’, which is consistent with the characteristic equation (Qn+1 = D). Conversely, the circuit operates as a memory mode when CLK is in logic ‘1’, meaning that the output Qn+1 remains in its current state Qn. Compared with D latch, an edge-triggered DFF with better anti-interference feature can be fabricated through two D latch elements in cascaded. Figure 5e shows the circuit schematic, optical image and measured waveforms of a falling edge-triggered DFF which consists of 12 BG-FETs in total. This circuit can immediately follow the data input D to output the correct logic signal (Qn+1 = D) at the falling edge of the control input CLK and hold the signal state (Qn+1 = Qn) until the next falling edge.

Additionally, combining flip-flop circuits and composite basic gate circuits can also implement other sequential logic functions for different applications. For example, a falling edge triggered TFF based on a characteristic equation (Qn+1 = T⊕Qn) can be fabricated by cascading an XOR gate at the D input terminal of DFF (that is, setting D = T⊕Qn), as shown in Fig. 5f. The output signal Qn+1 from the measured waveform flips once every time at the falling edge of control input CLK when data input T is logic ‘1’. Conversely, this TFF works in a memory mode when data input T is logic ‘0’. The TFF circuits can ensure the correct transmission of timing signals and also add a flipping function. Similarly, a flip-flop applied to the frequency-halving circuit is also shown as an example in Supplementary Fig. 13.
paper_content.methods:
Device fabrication
The BG-FETs and BG-FET-based logic circuits are built using the fabrication process compatible with silicon-based technology. First, the pad electrode and bottom electrodes are mapped in advance on the SiO /Si substrate using laser direct writing (Micro-Writer ML3) technology and proximity UV lithography (MA/BA6 Gen4) technology. Then 10/50 nm Cr/Au is deposited using thermal evaporation (PRO-Line PVD 200), followed by atomic-layer deposition (TALD-200) of a 20-nm-thickness HfO the dielectric layer. The CVD-grown monolayer MoS films are accurately stacked on the HfO using wet-transfer technology with polymethyl methacrylate film as a sacrificial layer. It is necessary to pattern the MoS film using the plasma etching (RLE-100R) technique with a mixture of O and SF to define the channel region. Subsequently, the designed drain and source electrodes are deposited based on e-beam lithography (EBL, FEI Quanta 3D) and thermal evaporation technology, and the ALD-grown HfO with a buffer layer of Sb O is deposited as the top gate dielectric. Where Sb O powder was evaporated by heating in the PVD system with a high vacuum (10-7 torr). The deposition rate is controlled to be 0.05 Å/s for the flat film with a thickness of 2-3 nm. Finally, the top bias-gated electrodes are deposited onto the designated position.

Electrical measurement
The electrical characteristics of the single BG-RFET devices and simple circuits are measured using a semiconductor parameter analyzer (Agilent B1500 coupled with six SMUs and two PMUs) in a vacuum probe station (Lake Shore). The measurements of complex digital circuits are performed by a semi-automatic probe station (SUMMIT200) connecting to a modular PXle SMU testing system (M9019A) equipped with six 5-channel source/measure units with 30 SMUs in total. All measurements for BG-FET, GLB and GLB-based logic circuits are conducted at room temperature.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The authors propose an asymmetric bias-gated MoS2 transistor and demonstrate a range of reconfigurable logic gates and small digital circuits built from these devices. The manuscript is well motivated, pursuing logic built purely from MoS2 transistors is an interesting direction, and the experimental demonstrations are impressive in scope. However, in its present form the paper has two major issues that hold me back from supporting publication: (1) the device novelty is limited relative to existing dual-gate/bias-gated MOSFET structures, and (2) the circuit benchmarks are incomplete and, in several respects, fail to support the claimed advantages (transistor-count saving and reconfigurability) compared to conventional CMOS. Below I list major concerns and specific, actionable suggestions to improve the manuscript.
1. Device novelty is limited. The proposed structure is equivalent to a conventional dual-gate MOSFET, where the top gate is connected to either the source or drain. Dual-gate MoS2 MOSFETs have already been reported (ACS Appl. Electron. Mater. 2020, 2, 111–119; Nat. Electron. 2, 563–571 (2019); 2021 IEDM, 10.1109/IEDM19574.2021.9720695). Moreover, such a configuration tends to degrade switching speed due to the increased capacitance between the top and bottom gate electrodes.
2. Extended source/drain design. The introduction of an extended drain or source region typically enhances short-channel effects in a MOSFET, which is generally undesirable. I understand that the authors intentionally introduced this feature to generate performance variation for digital circuit design, which is a creative idea. However, this approach appears to be a compromise to address the lack of an ideal complementary p-type transistor to the MoS2 NMOS. As a downgraded CMOS strategy, the authors should provide a more comprehensive comparison with conventional CMOS, including aspects such as scalability, speed, noise tolerance, and power efficiency, to justify its acceptability.
3. Reconfigurability concerns. (1) Although the circuits in Fig. 4 can be reconfigured to perform different functions, the reconfiguration appears to rely on manually rewiring the input/output, for example, VIN–P2 switching among B, A, and Ā. I assume this is achieved by altering probe connections. In a practical integrated circuit, such reconfiguration would require additional circuitry (e.g., multiplexers, inverters, or routing networks). Considering this overhead, the claimed advantage in transistor count saving may not hold. (2) For the digital circuits in Fig. 5, no on-chip reconfigurability is demonstrated, for example, dynamically switching the same circuit between D latch, D flip-flop, and T flip-flop functions.
4. Performance concerns. I appreciate the authors’ efforts to demonstrate various digital circuits. However, I remain concerned about their actual performance. For instance, the inverter’s threshold voltage (0.59 V) deviates significantly from the ideal mid-point (1 V), leading to poor noise margins. Additionally, all demonstrations operate at very low clock frequencies (< 1 Hz). Since transistor count reduction may trade off with performance degradation, a more comprehensive benchmarking, including switching speed, energy efficiency, and noise tolerance, is necessary.
5. Some minor issues.
(1) In Fig. 3a, what is VINbar? I assume it is fixed at 0 V. If not, additional circuits are required to generate it.
(2) In Fig. 4f, the waveform for A0 is missing.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This manuscript presents a bias-gated MoS₂ transistor platform that enables reconfigurable logic behavior within a unified, unipolar device framework. By strategically tuning the bias configuration at the source and drain terminals, the same MoS₂ FET can exhibit both enhancement- and depletion-type characteristics. Building on this mechanism, the authors construct a Generic Logic Block (GLB) capable of implementing multiple Boolean and sequential functions through electrical reconfiguration. The concept is technically sound and conceptually elegant, representing a well-balanced device-to-circuit co-design approach that advances the field toward programmable, CMOS-compatible 2D electronics. The experimental results convincingly validate the proposed mechanism across multiple logic hierarchies—including inverters, logic gates, arithmetic circuits, and flip-flops—and the fabrication strategy appropriately preserves 2D material integrity through low-thermal-budget bonding and passivation. Overall, this study offers a coherent and comprehensive demonstration of a scalable, reconfigurable, and doping-independent logic framework in 2D materials. I consider this manuscript a strong contribution suitable for publication in Nature Communications, subject to minor clarifications and refinements as outlined below.
1. Energy-band representation of bias-gated operation
The description of S-gated and D-gated operation modes is conceptually clear, but the accompanying energy-band diagrams are overly simplified. It is recommended to refine the schematic to more explicitly depict the spatial distribution of potential barriers and the corresponding modulation of threshold voltage in each configuration. A more detailed illustration—such as showing relative band alignment near the source and drain regions—would improve clarity and accessibility for a broad readership.
2. Benchmarking of inverter performance
The reported inverter gain of 157 is impressive for a 2D logic circuit. However, the discussion would benefit from benchmarking against representative results from prior 2D logic demonstrations or conventional CMOS technologies. A brief comparative analysis emphasizing key metrics such as gain, noise margin, and switching sharpness would help position the proposed GLB within the broader context of state-of-the-art 2D logic performance.
3. Dynamic reconfigurability demonstration
The reconfigurability of the GLB is effectively shown through static bias configurations, but its dynamic behavior remains unexplored. Including a brief experiment or supplementary figure demonstrating real-time switching between two logic modes (e.g., AND ↔ OR) would substantially strengthen the claim of electrical reconfigurability and distinguish this platform from previously reported static architectures.
4. Scalability and energy considerations
The scalability and energy implications of the bias-gated architecture are not yet discussed. It would be valuable to include a short paragraph commenting on potential challenges—such as leakage current, bias overhead, and interconnect complexity—when scaling to higher integration levels. This discussion would provide a more comprehensive view of the feasibility of extending the GLB concept toward large-scale reconfigurable 2D logic systems.
5. System-level circuit considerations
The demonstration of sequential circuits (D-latch, D-flip-flop, and T-flip-flop) serves as a meaningful validation of the GLB concept. Nevertheless, the discussion could be strengthened by addressing signal propagation, synchronization, and timing stability when cascading multiple GLBs in larger logic networks. A brief consideration of signal restoration, clock distribution, and potential strategies for maintaining bias uniformity would enhance the manuscript’s system-level perspective.
6. Static power characterization
To more clearly elucidate the static power consumption characteristics of the proposed logic circuit, it is recommended that the authors provide the dependence of the inverter current (Idd) on the input voltage during operation. This would give a more complete picture of power behavior under different biasing conditions.
7. Scaling and frequency limits
To further underscore the technological potential of this approach, a concise theoretical discussion on the ultimate scaling limits of the device dimensions and the upper frequency bound of circuit operation is encouraged. Such analysis would help clarify the long-term prospects of this bias-gated architecture.
8. Full-swing output characteristics
Finally, it is recommended that the authors elaborate on the mechanism responsible for achieving full-swing voltage output in the logic circuit. A more detailed explanation would help emphasize the advantage of the proposed approach over conventional NMOS-based designs, which typically exhibit threshold voltage–related signal degradation.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Summary
This research presents an asymmetric MoS2 FET architecture as a foundation for high-density reconfigurable logic. MoS2 FET has been demonstrated into a generic logic block. MoS2-based GLB reduced the transistor count by over sixty percent versus equivalent CMOS circuits. Simple bias control toggles operation between source-gated and drain-gated modes. The block dynamically implements various logic functions, including inverter, half adder, multiplexer, encoder, and SRAM within one circuit. While the work is well-structured and the data are compelling, several points require clarification and revision before the manuscript can be deemed suitable for publication in this journal.
Major comments
1. The manuscript provides insufficient information regarding Sb2O3. Unlike HfO2, Sb2O3 is not a commonly used dielectric material. Therefore, the authors should clarify why it was chosen, specify its thickness, and cite appropriate references [1, 2] that support its use. In addition, detailed information on the deposition process of the Sb2O3 buffer layer during device fabrication is required.
2. The authors seem to emphasize the advantage of the van der Waals interface formed by Sb2O3 to enhance device performance. If that is the case, why was this material applied only in the top-gate configuration? In the BG inverter, part of the channel electrons accumulated on the upper side may indeed benefit from a clean interface, whereas in the Ref inverter, all channel electrons accumulate at the bottom interface, which is likely degraded by the ALD-grown HfO2. This raises concerns about the fairness of the comparison, as the two devices may not be under equivalent interfacial conditions.
3. In Figure 3c, the authors compare the gain of the BG and Ref inverters only at VDD = 2 V, while Figures 3d and 3e present parameters solely for the BG inverter. Can the authors confirm that the BG inverter still shows similar or superior performance compared to the Ref inverter across all VDD values when considering parameters such as VM, gain, Pstatic, peak, and NM/VDD? A more comprehensive comparison, like Supplementary Figure 1, seems necessary. Moreover, including the V₍M₎ shift of 0.06 V (mentioned in Supplementary Figure 2b) directly in Figure 3d would make the data presentation more compelling.
4. It would be beneficial to show the corresponding IOUT values for VIN = 0.9 V and 1.0 V in Supplementary Figure 2a. The current crop graph looks incomplete and visually unappealing.

Reply: We thank the reviewer’s comments and we agree that conventional dual-gate MoS MOSFETs have already been reported from various research perspectives, as mentioned by the reviewer. However, our bias-gated device structure is fundamentally different from conventional dual-gate MOSFET.
And we agree that the dual-gate configuration may degrade switching speed, mainly due to the RC delay in dynamic switching process. RC delay depends on the value of the parasitic resistance and capacitance where the capacitance is mainly determined by the device size. However, as the dimension of transistors continues to downscale to enable higher integration density, the capacitance and resistance of single transistor will sharply decrease1,2. At the circuit level, the switching speed or dynamic power mainly depends on the number of transistors. Notably, there is no capacitance between the top gate and the source or drain of our BG-FET due to the short-circuit.
Finally, we thank the reviewer again for this important point, the dynamic characteristics of multi-field gated MOSFETs deserve further investigation in the future.

I appreciate the authors’ efforts in performing additional dynamic characterization, which makes the overall characterization more complete. However, I still have two concerns regarding the authors’ response.
Regarding my Comment 2:
The authors appear to argue that the bias-gate design can potentially improve, rather than worsen, short-channel effects. However, they do not provide a clear explanation of how the bias-gate design modifies specific short-channel effects, such as drain-induced barrier lowering. Instead, they rely on comparisons to extended source/drain designs in silicon CMOS technology and the gate-all-around technique in 2D semiconductor channels (Ref. 5) to justify the role of their bias-gate design. These device architectures are fundamentally different from the bias-gate structure proposed in this paper, where the source/drain region is connected to a short gate. Therefore, it is not valid to use effects observed in these other architectures to explain the role of the bias-gate design in the short-channel regime of the proposed device.
Furthermore, References 3-4 discuss thin-film source-gated transistors, whose architecture also differs significantly from that of a typical MOSFET. These devices utilize Schottky contacts and rely on the resulting depletion regions to suppress short-channel effects. This operating principle is not applicable to the bias-gate structure proposed here. Citing these irrelevant device designs and references to defend the proposed mechanism is misleading and inappropriate, which undermines the technical credibility of the work.
Regarding my Comment 3:
Thanks for the clarification on the device characterization. It is now clear that the proposed GLB is effectively a 6-input, 2-output system. Nevertheless, this raises a more fundamental concern: how can the relationships among the different inputs be well-defined and enforced in a practical integrated-circuit implementation?
The gates demonstrated in Fig. 4 are mostly 2-input, 1-output blocks. Since only two inputs are logically required, defining and maintaining the relationships among the remaining four inputs will inevitably require additional circuitry. For example, in the AND/NAND case, Vin-p1 and Vin-p3 are inverted versions of each other, which would require an inverter. In contrast, in the 2-to-1 MUX case, Vin-p1 and Vin-p3 must be independent signals. Similarly, Vin-p2 and Vin-c are identical for AND/NAND but inverted for OR/NOR, etc. Reconfiguring these inputs would require switches to manage shorted connections, inversions, or disconnections, necessitating additional circuitry.
This highlights a significant overhead cost for the claimed “reconfigurable logic.” The current demonstration does not account for the peripheral circuits required to generate and manage these input relationships. These circuits are critical for achieving true reconfigurability, but they are neither explicitly presented nor discussed. Consequently, whether the proposed reconfigurability actually leads to a reduced transistor count in practical implementation remains an unanswered question.

## Abstract

Integrating two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors and CMOS technology is a promising pathway for next-generation integrated circuits. However, the implementation of this strategy is hindered by the limited polarity modulation of 2D semiconductors and the inherent characteristics of CMOS architectures. Here, we report a generic logic block (GLB) that uses bias-gated molybdenum disulfide transistors (BG-FET). The BG-FETs exhibit threshold-adaptive field-effect characteristics through simple bias manipulation, enabling good rail-to-rail operation in the inverter circuits. The GLB composed of four BG-FETs can perform reconfigurable logic operations in a single circuit, including basic gate circuits, half-adder, multiplexer, encoder and static-random-access-memory. In contrast, conventional CMOS circuits require at least 100 transistors to perform the same set of operations. We further integrate flip-flop circuits and arithmetic logic units by cascading as-fabricated GLBs, featuring a transistor count saving of over 60% compared to CMOS design. Collectively, BG-FET-based GLB emerges as a post-CMOS integration technology with compelling potential.

---

## Introduction

Two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors still maintain excellent electrical characteristics even at sub-nanometer scales and offer the potential for further extending the logic device scaling1-6. But its potential is severely hampered by the lack of proper logic architecture. The current silicon-based CMOS (complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor) architecture realized by high-energy doping technology is not suitable for atomically thin 2D semiconductors. So far, various doping methods have been developed to tune the polarity of 2D transistors7-9. But effective techniques towards practical circuit-level manufacture still lack because there is little physical space for impurity dopants in such atomically thin lattice10. Therefore, most large-scale logic circuits based on 2D semiconductors developed to date primarily follow the non-complementary NMOS architecture11-14, which inherently exhibit higher power consumption than CMOS technology. More importantly, an inherent problem is that logic functions implemented in CMOS or NMOS architecture require a large number of transistors, which hinders the processes of chip area scaling-down and function integration. Consequently, a necessity has been awakened to develop integrated device architectures based on the intrinsic advantages of 2D materials.

The emerging reconfigurable technology15, in which a transistor can be dynamically programmed to function as either an n- or p-FET during run-time by applying an external control voltage, presents a promising approach beyond CMOS. Reconfigurable circuits can achieve higher logic function density compared to CMOS architecture, thereby improving transistor utilization and reducing circuit redundancy. However, the reconfigurable field-effect transistor (RFET) relies on the modulation of device polarity, transitioning from ambipolar type to either n- or p- type, which necessitates additional hardware resources to implement16-19. This will result in additional power consumption and problems with circuit complexity. Moreover, the implementation of Boolean functions in the RFET-based circuits with full-swing output still follows a CMOS-like configuration20, utilizing p-FETs and n-FETs for pull-up and pull-down networks, respectively. This approach does not contribute to reducing the overall transistor count. Alternatively, reconfigurable circuit elements based on 2D homo- or heterostructure device21-23 and 2D single-transistor-based logic elements using a vertical- or split-dual-gate design24-27 are widely recognized as effective strategies to simplify circuits. However, these reconfigurable circuits are limited to small set of few fundamental logic operations and are further constrained by the intrinsic polarity or thickness of 2D semiconductors.

In this article, we report a bias-gated FET (BG-FET, Fig. 1a) designed to integrate generic logic blocks (GLBs). The asymmetric bias-gated device architecture enables BG-FETs to possess threshold-adaptive field-effect characteristics through different bias modes (source-gated or drain-gated, Fig. 1b). Leveraging these unique structural and electrical features, firstly, a cascaded logic inverter consisting of two BG-FETs with identical process parameters is fabricated to achieve good rail-to-rail operation. Subsequently, within a circuit composed of four BG-FETs, we design and fabricate a GLB with full-equivalent input/output (I/O) ports for performing dynamic reconfigurable logic computing by programming different combinations of input signals (Fig. 1c), including basic gate circuits, half-adder, multiplexer (MUX), encoder and static random-access memory (SRAM). As a benchmark comparison, implementing these functions in CMOS design typically requires more than 100 transistors (Fig. 1d). The as-fabricated GLBs are further used to integrate multiple arithmetic logic units and sequential circuit units with a transistor count reduction of over 60% compared to CMOS design, such as 2-bit multipliers and edge-triggered flip-flops.

## Results

Characterization of the unipolar MoS BG-FET
2
A schematic of the BG-FET device concept is shown in Fig. 2a. The basic structure consists of a unipolar CVD-grown monolayer MoS channel sandwiched between hafnium oxide and antimony oxide (HfO /MoS /Sb O /HfO ), as well as a fully back-gated bottom electrode and a locally unilateral bias-gated top electrode. To confirm the signature device structure of our BG-FET, a representative sample and a traditional MOSFET for reference (Ref. FET) are simultaneously fabricated based on a same MoS film (Fig. 2b). The fabrication processes (see in Methods) of two devices are completely identical, except that an asymmetrically extended bias-gated electrode is added to the BG-FET. Notably, we choose a van der Waals crystal Sb O as a buffer layer to form a high-quality oxide-to-semiconductor interface28-30, enabling the integration of high-κ dielectrics via atomic layer deposition. Moreover, a van der Waals gate dielectric interface can better maintain the intrinsic properties of the underlying 2D materials, which also helpful for improving the uniformity and stability of 2D electronics.

The asymmetrical nature of this as-fabricated BG-FET is defined as two different bias schemes: extended bias-gated electrode as source (named source-gated, S-Gated) and as drain (named drain-gated, D-Gated). In principle, the energy band diagrams under two operating modes are shown in Fig. 2c. In S-Gated mode, the channel electrons around the source contact are depleted due to the bias-gated electrostatic (negative potential relative to the drain), resulting in the extension of the electron injection barrier compared to the Ref. FET. The widened barrier can block the injection of electrons from the source, thus requiring a larger V . In D-Gated mode, the accumulated electrons can improve the channel conductivity around the drain contact due to the bias-gated electrostatic (positive potential relative to the source), but not affecting the electron injection barrier at the source.

In detailed comparison, the electrical properties of two devices are investigated under the same testing conditions. As shown in Fig. 2d, the saturation voltage (V ) of BG-FET is smaller under the same gate voltage (V ) compared with the Ref. FET. By definition, the V corresponds to the drain-source voltage (V ) at which the drain-source current (I ) reaches saturation, equivalent to the V required for transistor pinch-off. Figure 2e illustrates the pinch-off mechanism of BG-FET and Ref. FET. As V increases, the depletion region of Ref. FET occurs at drain until the channel is pinched off and V is defined. In S-Gated mode, however, the depletion of BG-FET occurs both in drain and source due to the extended bias-gated electrode31,32. The source-side depletion region progressively expands towards the drain with the increasing V due to the bias-gated electrostatic (maintained at a negative potential relative to the drain), enabling the BG-FET to be pinched off prematurely and a smaller V is defined. Figure 2f exhibits the transfer characteristics of two devices both with a high on-off ratio of >109 and a low off-state current of less than 0.1 pA. Noticeably, the V (reference voltage, defined as the V required when the I is equal to 1 nA) in S-Gated mode is offset by around 0.7 V in the forward (right) direction compared to Ref. FET. A larger V for BG-FET is required to achieve the same current due to the bias-gated device structure. The maximum difference of I under the same V exceeds three orders of magnitude in the sub-threshold region. As the V increases, this difference gradually decreases and tends to be consistent, because the electron density in the channel is gradually dominated by V . The V -dependent V , R and more experimental data of two devices are demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. 1. These obvious differences between two devices indicate the effectiveness of the bias-gated structure design.

More valuable is that the asymmetric bias-gated device architecture enables BG-FETs to possess threshold-adaptive field-effect characteristics, which is crucial for subsequent GLB circuit design. To verify the inherent robustness of this characteristic and assess its scalability for large-scale integration, we fabricate an array of 256 BG-FETs distributed across 16 dies, with each die integrating 16 individual devices (Supplementary Fig. 2). All devices were fabricated on a continuous single-crystal MoS₂ thin film33 under identical process parameters. Subsequently, four BG-FETs were randomly selected from four units in each die for electrical characterization, yielding a total of 64 devices spread out to study uniformity over a large area. The transfer characteristics of BG-FETs under D-Gated and S-Gated modes are tested, as shown in Fig. 2g. The transistors exhibit a desired uniformity and threshold-adaptive field-effect characteristics. Besides, the statistical histogram of V difference in two modes is concentrated between 0.54-0.6 V (see the inset of Fig. 2g), indicating a low device-to-device variability.

To further explore the stability of BG-FETs, we electrically characterized the as-fabricated devices placed in the vacuum atmosphere for 1 week, 4 weeks, and 7 weeks. As shown in Fig. 2h, the BG-FET maintain excellent threshold-adaptive field-effect characteristics after seven weeks, and the ΔV of approximately 0.57 V between the two operating modes shows negligible variation throughout this period. And the BG-FET exhibit impressive threshold-adaptive field-effect characteristics even at high temperature of 400 K, as shown in Fig. 2i. Note that the threshold voltage of the BG-FET exhibits a negative shift with increasing temperature. This phenomenon can be attributed to the enhanced thermal activation of free carriers at elevated temperatures34,35. Furthermore, a larger shift amplitude is observed in S-Gated mode, leading to a progressive decrease in ΔV . This may be due to the release of more free carriers bound by the widened barrier induced by bias-gated electrostatic at high temperatures. The desired uniformity and stability of BG-FETs can be attributed to the bias-gated structure design with a built-in packaging function for maintaining the integrity of the channel materials, except for the high stability of the grown MoS .

Logic inverter based on unipolar MoS BG-FET
2
The inverter (NOT gate) that performs the Boolean function Y = A̅ is a basic logic element in digital circuits, in which A̅ is defined as an opposite voltage level to input A. Figure 3a shows the schematic of an adaptive-switching logic inverter composed of two as-fabricated unipolar MoS BG-FETs in series. In reported MoS -based inverter circuits11,12,36,37, specific designs are required for the driver and load devices to achieve rail-to-rail operation, such as different width/length (W/L) ratios, metal gates or channel materials between two transistors. In our demonstration, the as-fabricated SG-FET as driver (BG-FET in S-Gated mode) and DG-FET as load (BG-FET in D-Gated mode) can be dynamically switched through simple voltage manipulation.

To further clarify the role of a bias-gated device structure in digital circuits, two inverters made of BG-FETs and Ref. FETs are fabricated, respectively (Fig. 3b). The four devices used to fabricate two inverters have the same size and are based on a same single-layer MoS . Figure 3c shows the typical voltage transfer curves (VTCs) of two inverters with different switching threshold voltage (V ) at V = 2 V. The V of the BG-FET-based inverter (BG-inverter) shifts from approximately -0.15 V to 0.59 V compared with Ref. FET-based inverter (Ref.-inverter), which indicates that BG-inverter can realize good rail-to-rail operation due to the threshold-adaptive field-effect characteristics of BG-FET. Noticeably, an inverter that loses the cascaded function due to input and output not in the same range is strictly referred to as an invalid circuit. As mentioned above, the reported inverters require a specific design to achieve rail-to-rail operation, however, which cannot change the function of the constituent components (load or driver) once built.

More detailed static characteristics of the BG-inverter and Ref. inverter under different V are shown in Supplementary Fig. 3. Two inverters show similar performance for the parameters of gain and I across all V values. Where a peak gain of 157 for BG-inverter and of 159 for Ref. inverter, a peak I of less than 2 nA for BG-inverter and of less than 5 nA for Ref. inverter are achieved at V = 5 V. And the key parameters of BG-inverter, such as peak gain, V , noise margin (N /V ) and peak static power are intuitively shown in Fig. 3d-e. A total noise margin (NM + NM )/V over 85% and a low static power (P ) of less than 10 nW across all V values are calculated. And The V shift of 0.06 V for BG-inverter under different V is observed, which may be attributed to the ΔV variation of BG-FET under different V . In theory, the competition relationship between bias-gated and back-gated modulation can be controlled by optimizing the L /L ratios, in which L and L are defined as the length of the bias-gated electrode and the channel in Fig. 2a, respectively. As this ratio increases, the control region of the bias-gated electrode expands relatively. The controllable modulation of this competition relationship allows for the on-demand design of application-oriented devices.

Additionally, the BG-inverter can maintain a full-swing output response at a 2 V full-scale square input signal of 100 Hz, even after 1,000 switching cycles (Figure 3f). The dynamic switching speed mainly determined by the RC delay (𝜏) is also a very significant evaluation indicator in logic circuits. To further characterize this performance, the dynamic switching behavior of the BG-inverter by using an AC input signal is studied at higher frequencies (Supplementary Fig. 4). As demonstrated by the dynamic analysis, the inverter can immediately invert the input signal, and the output signal can maintain a high-quality waveform response that is opposite to the input signal at a relatively low frequency (<500 Hz). However, the output waveform gradually deformed with the frequency of the input signal increases, and full-swing output cannot be achieved at a higher frequency (>5 kHz) mainly due to a RC delay in dynamic switching. A rising time delay (𝜏 ) of 285 µs and falling time delay (𝜏 ) of 35 µs are extracted at 1 kHz, where the delay 𝜏 is defined as the time intervals between 10% and 90% of V , as shown in Fig. 3g. These performance metrics of the BG-inverters demonstrate competitive results at the current device scale compared with state-of-the-art 2D materials-based CMOS inverters (Supplementary Table 1). There remains significant potential for further optimization through continued device engineering and process refinement.

This GLB can perform logic functions with six input terminals (V , V , V , V , V and V̅̅̅̅̅̅) and two output terminals (V and V ). In this circuit, the 4-bit input signals: (0001), (0010), (0100), and (1000) are encoded as 2-bit binary codes: (00), (01), (10), and (11), respectively, which are consistent with the function truth table of the 4-2 encoder (Supplementary Fig. 8). Noteworthy, the GLB circuit can fully implement all logic functions with a full-swing output voltage due to the threshold-adaptive field-effect characteristics of BG-FET. The principle is analogous to the complementary structure in CMOS technology. More detailed explanation seen in Supplementary Fig. 10.

To further verify the feasibility of GLB using BG-FET device architecture for digital circuit optimization, various arithmetic logic units (ALU) and sequential circuit units are integrated on the monolayer MoS film. Figure 5a shows the schematics and optical image of a 2-bit carry-save-adder (CSA) multiplier that consists of four GLBs and four BG-inverters with 24 BG-FETs in total. By analyzing the principle of multiplication (depicted in Supplementary Fig. 11a), it is found that the partial products can be achieved through logic AND gates (Y = AB). While the sum of partial products can be achieved through adder circuits. Based on this principle, two GLBs are reconstructed as four AND gates to implement four partial products, two GLBs are reconstructed as two half-adders for partial product summation and four embedded BG-inverters are used to provide necessary complementary signals. The measured output voltage signals (P , P , P , P ) are shown in Fig. 5b, indicating that GLB-based 2-bit CSA-multiplier can fully implement multiplication operations according to the truth table (shown in Supplementary Fig. 11b) for all the input combinations (A , A , B , B ). CSA multiplier circuits that can improve the speed of data processing and enable more complex data analysis with efficient computing play an important part in digital ICs. Furthermore, the circuit design, optical image and measured results for 1-bit digital comparator, controllable left/right shifter and 1-bit full-adder based on BG-FETs are also plotted as examples in Supplementary Fig. 12. The output voltage signals can correctly respond to all possible input combinations according to the truth table.

The sequential logic elements are critical components in memory and data manipulation circuits for digital ICs. Figure 5c shows the status table of D latch, D flip-flop (DFF) and T flip-flop (TFF), in which signal CLK as the global clock control input, signal D as the data input and signal Q as the output. The circuit design, optical image and measured waveforms of the D latch based on two BG-FETs and a SRAM reconstructed by GLB are plotted in Fig. 5d. In this sequential circuit, the output Qn+1 is seen to follow the input D when the input CLK is in logic ‘0’, which is consistent with the characteristic equation (Qn+1 = D). Conversely, the circuit operates as a memory mode when CLK is in logic ‘1’, meaning that the output Qn+1 remains in its current state Qn. Compared with D latch, an edge-triggered DFF with better anti-interference feature can be fabricated through two D latch elements in cascaded. Figure 5e shows the circuit schematic, optical image and measured waveforms of a falling edge-triggered DFF which consists of 12 BG-FETs in total. This circuit can immediately follow the data input D to output the correct logic signal (Qn+1 = D) at the falling edge of the control input CLK and hold the signal state (Qn+1 = Qn) until the next falling edge.

Additionally, combining flip-flop circuits and composite basic gate circuits can also implement other sequential logic functions for different applications. For example, a falling edge triggered TFF based on a characteristic equation (Qn+1 = T⊕Qn) can be fabricated by cascading an XOR gate at the D input terminal of DFF (that is, setting D = T⊕Qn), as shown in Fig. 5f. The output signal Qn+1 from the measured waveform flips once every time at the falling edge of control input CLK when data input T is logic ‘1’. Conversely, this TFF works in a memory mode when data input T is logic ‘0’. The TFF circuits can ensure the correct transmission of timing signals and also add a flipping function. Similarly, a flip-flop applied to the frequency-halving circuit is also shown as an example in Supplementary Fig. 13.

## Methods

Device fabrication
The BG-FETs and BG-FET-based logic circuits are built using the fabrication process compatible with silicon-based technology. First, the pad electrode and bottom electrodes are mapped in advance on the SiO /Si substrate using laser direct writing (Micro-Writer ML3) technology and proximity UV lithography (MA/BA6 Gen4) technology. Then 10/50 nm Cr/Au is deposited using thermal evaporation (PRO-Line PVD 200), followed by atomic-layer deposition (TALD-200) of a 20-nm-thickness HfO the dielectric layer. The CVD-grown monolayer MoS films are accurately stacked on the HfO using wet-transfer technology with polymethyl methacrylate film as a sacrificial layer. It is necessary to pattern the MoS film using the plasma etching (RLE-100R) technique with a mixture of O and SF to define the channel region. Subsequently, the designed drain and source electrodes are deposited based on e-beam lithography (EBL, FEI Quanta 3D) and thermal evaporation technology, and the ALD-grown HfO with a buffer layer of Sb O is deposited as the top gate dielectric. Where Sb O powder was evaporated by heating in the PVD system with a high vacuum (10-7 torr). The deposition rate is controlled to be 0.05 Å/s for the flat film with a thickness of 2-3 nm. Finally, the top bias-gated electrodes are deposited onto the designated position.

Electrical measurement
The electrical characteristics of the single BG-RFET devices and simple circuits are measured using a semiconductor parameter analyzer (Agilent B1500 coupled with six SMUs and two PMUs) in a vacuum probe station (Lake Shore). The measurements of complex digital circuits are performed by a semi-automatic probe station (SUMMIT200) connecting to a modular PXle SMU testing system (M9019A) equipped with six 5-channel source/measure units with 30 SMUs in total. All measurements for BG-FET, GLB and GLB-based logic circuits are conducted at room temperature.

The authors propose an asymmetric bias-gated MoS2 transistor and demonstrate a range of reconfigurable logic gates and small digital circuits built from these devices. The manuscript is well motivated, pursuing logic built purely from MoS2 transistors is an interesting direction, and the experimental demonstrations are impressive in scope. However, in its present form the paper has two major issues that hold me back from supporting publication: (1) the device novelty is limited relative to existing dual-gate/bias-gated MOSFET structures, and (2) the circuit benchmarks are incomplete and, in several respects, fail to support the claimed advantages (transistor-count saving and reconfigurability) compared to conventional CMOS. Below I list major concerns and specific, actionable suggestions to improve the manuscript.
1. Device novelty is limited. The proposed structure is equivalent to a conventional dual-gate MOSFET, where the top gate is connected to either the source or drain. Dual-gate MoS2 MOSFETs have already been reported (ACS Appl. Electron. Mater. 2020, 2, 111–119; Nat. Electron. 2, 563–571 (2019); 2021 IEDM, 10.1109/IEDM19574.2021.9720695). Moreover, such a configuration tends to degrade switching speed due to the increased capacitance between the top and bottom gate electrodes.
2. Extended source/drain design. The introduction of an extended drain or source region typically enhances short-channel effects in a MOSFET, which is generally undesirable. I understand that the authors intentionally introduced this feature to generate performance variation for digital circuit design, which is a creative idea. However, this approach appears to be a compromise to address the lack of an ideal complementary p-type transistor to the MoS2 NMOS. As a downgraded CMOS strategy, the authors should provide a more comprehensive comparison with conventional CMOS, including aspects such as scalability, speed, noise tolerance, and power efficiency, to justify its acceptability.
3. Reconfigurability concerns. (1) Although the circuits in Fig. 4 can be reconfigured to perform different functions, the reconfiguration appears to rely on manually rewiring the input/output, for example, VIN–P2 switching among B, A, and Ā. I assume this is achieved by altering probe connections. In a practical integrated circuit, such reconfiguration would require additional circuitry (e.g., multiplexers, inverters, or routing networks). Considering this overhead, the claimed advantage in transistor count saving may not hold. (2) For the digital circuits in Fig. 5, no on-chip reconfigurability is demonstrated, for example, dynamically switching the same circuit between D latch, D flip-flop, and T flip-flop functions.
4. Performance concerns. I appreciate the authors’ efforts to demonstrate various digital circuits. However, I remain concerned about their actual performance. For instance, the inverter’s threshold voltage (0.59 V) deviates significantly from the ideal mid-point (1 V), leading to poor noise margins. Additionally, all demonstrations operate at very low clock frequencies (< 1 Hz). Since transistor count reduction may trade off with performance degradation, a more comprehensive benchmarking, including switching speed, energy efficiency, and noise tolerance, is necessary.

(1) In Fig. 3a, what is VINbar? I assume it is fixed at 0 V. If not, additional circuits are required to generate it.

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript presents a bias-gated MoS₂ transistor platform that enables reconfigurable logic behavior within a unified, unipolar device framework. By strategically tuning the bias configuration at the source and drain terminals, the same MoS₂ FET can exhibit both enhancement- and depletion-type characteristics. Building on this mechanism, the authors construct a Generic Logic Block (GLB) capable of implementing multiple Boolean and sequential functions through electrical reconfiguration. The concept is technically sound and conceptually elegant, representing a well-balanced device-to-circuit co-design approach that advances the field toward programmable, CMOS-compatible 2D electronics. The experimental results convincingly validate the proposed mechanism across multiple logic hierarchies—including inverters, logic gates, arithmetic circuits, and flip-flops—and the fabrication strategy appropriately preserves 2D material integrity through low-thermal-budget bonding and passivation. Overall, this study offers a coherent and comprehensive demonstration of a scalable, reconfigurable, and doping-independent logic framework in 2D materials. I consider this manuscript a strong contribution suitable for publication in Nature Communications, subject to minor clarifications and refinements as outlined below.
1. Energy-band representation of bias-gated operation
The description of S-gated and D-gated operation modes is conceptually clear, but the accompanying energy-band diagrams are overly simplified. It is recommended to refine the schematic to more explicitly depict the spatial distribution of potential barriers and the corresponding modulation of threshold voltage in each configuration. A more detailed illustration—such as showing relative band alignment near the source and drain regions—would improve clarity and accessibility for a broad readership.
2. Benchmarking of inverter performance
The reported inverter gain of 157 is impressive for a 2D logic circuit. However, the discussion would benefit from benchmarking against representative results from prior 2D logic demonstrations or conventional CMOS technologies. A brief comparative analysis emphasizing key metrics such as gain, noise margin, and switching sharpness would help position the proposed GLB within the broader context of state-of-the-art 2D logic performance.
3. Dynamic reconfigurability demonstration
The reconfigurability of the GLB is effectively shown through static bias configurations, but its dynamic behavior remains unexplored. Including a brief experiment or supplementary figure demonstrating real-time switching between two logic modes (e.g., AND ↔ OR) would substantially strengthen the claim of electrical reconfigurability and distinguish this platform from previously reported static architectures.
4. Scalability and energy considerations
The scalability and energy implications of the bias-gated architecture are not yet discussed. It would be valuable to include a short paragraph commenting on potential challenges—such as leakage current, bias overhead, and interconnect complexity—when scaling to higher integration levels. This discussion would provide a more comprehensive view of the feasibility of extending the GLB concept toward large-scale reconfigurable 2D logic systems.
5. System-level circuit considerations
The demonstration of sequential circuits (D-latch, D-flip-flop, and T-flip-flop) serves as a meaningful validation of the GLB concept. Nevertheless, the discussion could be strengthened by addressing signal propagation, synchronization, and timing stability when cascading multiple GLBs in larger logic networks. A brief consideration of signal restoration, clock distribution, and potential strategies for maintaining bias uniformity would enhance the manuscript’s system-level perspective.
6. Static power characterization
To more clearly elucidate the static power consumption characteristics of the proposed logic circuit, it is recommended that the authors provide the dependence of the inverter current (Idd) on the input voltage during operation. This would give a more complete picture of power behavior under different biasing conditions.
7. Scaling and frequency limits
To further underscore the technological potential of this approach, a concise theoretical discussion on the ultimate scaling limits of the device dimensions and the upper frequency bound of circuit operation is encouraged. Such analysis would help clarify the long-term prospects of this bias-gated architecture.
8. Full-swing output characteristics
Finally, it is recommended that the authors elaborate on the mechanism responsible for achieving full-swing voltage output in the logic circuit. A more detailed explanation would help emphasize the advantage of the proposed approach over conventional NMOS-based designs, which typically exhibit threshold voltage–related signal degradation.
